syllabus.raw:
Gradient descent
Newton's method
Armijo line search
Quasi-Newton / BFGS
Gram–Schmidt
Conjugate gradient

lesson.oneLiner: Walk downhill along the negative gradient and let the learning rate decide how far each step goes.
lesson.why: The direction tells you where to go; the step size controls how far. A long jump can land higher on the other side of the valley.
lesson.analogy: Descend a dark valley one careful step at a time instead of one heroic leap.

pitfalls.text: A step that is too large can overshoot the minimum and raise the objective.

notesGaps: Your notes state the rule but never the decision: what to try first when a large downhill step lands higher.
lesson.takeaway: The direction tells you where to go. Step size controls how far you go. Armijo checks for sufficient decrease.
lesson.distinction: A locally downhill direction does not guarantee a downhill result for a large step.

examQuestion.q: A gradient step points downhill but increases the objective. Explain two distinct reasons and the fix for each.
examQuestion.modelAnswer: Oversized step: reduce the learning rate or backtrack until the Armijo condition holds. Non-descent direction (bad scaling or curvature): recheck the gradient or switch to a curvature-aware preconditioner.

lesson.oneLiner: A local curvature model helps choose the update.
lesson.why: Newton uses curvature directly, so steps can be far shorter than plain gradient descent near the solution.
lesson.analogy: Feel the shape of the ground underfoot, not just the slope at one point.
lesson.takeaway: Newton uses curvature directly. BFGS updates an approximation.
lesson.distinction: Newton uses curvature directly. BFGS updates an approximation.

examQuestion.q: When is the Newton update undefined?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: When the local curvature (f'' or the Hessian) is zero or singular, the update cannot divide through — fall back to a gradient or regularized step.

lesson.oneLiner: Accept a candidate step when it produces sufficient decrease relative to the local slope and step size.
lesson.why: A lower objective value alone can still fail the test — Armijo ties the decrease to the slope you promised.
lesson.analogy: A discount only counts if it is big enough for the distance you drove.
notesGaps: Your notes copy the condition name but not the comparison against the local slope.
lesson.takeaway: A lower objective value alone can still fail the Armijo test.
lesson.distinction: Any decrease is not enough; the decrease must be sufficient for the candidate step and local slope.

examQuestion.q: Does any decrease in the objective satisfy Armijo?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: No. Armijo requires f(x + t d) ≤ f(x) + c t ∇f·d for the trial step t; a tiny decrease can fail.

lesson.oneLiner: Use changes in position and gradient to update a curvature approximation.
lesson.why: You get Newton-like steps without computing or inverting the true Hessian every iteration.
lesson.analogy: Keep a running sketch of the terrain from the last few walks instead of re-surveying the whole hill.
notesGaps: Your notes paste the update formula without the intuition the exam question would test.
lesson.takeaway: The update reuses information from earlier steps.
lesson.distinction: BFGS never forms the true Hessian — it refines an approximation from position and gradient changes.

examQuestion.q: What two quantities does the BFGS update use from the last step?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: The change in position (s = x_{k+1} − x_k) and the change in gradient (y = ∇f_{k+1} − ∇f_k).

lesson.oneLiner: Build orthogonal directions by subtracting projections onto directions you already built.
lesson.why: Orthogonal bases make lengths and coefficients behave; your notes contain no matched passage for this topic.
lesson.analogy: Straighten a stack of leaning poles one at a time, each trimmed square against all before it.
notesGaps: No matching passage in these notes — this card is Vertex's explanation, not your text.
lesson.takeaway: Orthogonal vectors have zero dot product. Orthonormal vectors also have unit length.
lesson.distinction: Orthogonal vectors have zero dot product. Orthonormal vectors also have unit length.

examQuestion.q: State the difference between orthogonal and orthonormal sets.
examQuestion.modelAnswer: Orthogonal: pairwise dot products are zero. Orthonormal: additionally every vector has unit length.

lesson.oneLiner: For a symmetric positive-definite linear system, build search directions conjugate with respect to the system matrix.
lesson.why: Each new direction keeps the previous ones optimal instead of undoing them — your notes contain no matched passage.
lesson.analogy: Cut a cake into slices that never re-trim the cuts you already made.
notesGaps: No matching passage in these notes — this card is Vertex's explanation, not your text.
lesson.takeaway: Conjugacy uses the matrix-weighted inner product.
lesson.distinction: Conjugate directions are orthogonal under the matrix-weighted inner product, not the plain dot product.

examQuestion.q: What property must the system matrix have for standard conjugate gradient?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: Symmetric positive definite — it guarantees the quadratic being minimized is bowl-shaped and the directions stay descent.
